---
title: "How SimpleFOC works"
---

The firmware in [FAAV-G431-ESC](https://github.com/MIT-AURA-Lab/FAAV-G431-ESC)
is a [SimpleFOC](https://docs.simplefoc.com) application. This page is what you
need to read that firmware and change it with confidence: what the library
computes, in what order, and where your settings enter. It is background for
[Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd) and [Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd), not
a procedure.

## The problem it solves

A brushless motor has three windings and no brushes, so nothing decides on its
own which winding should be energised. Something has to look at where the rotor
is and energise the windings to put the stator's magnetic field about **90°
ahead** of the rotor's magnets, the orientation that produces the most
torque per amp. Do that continuously and the motor behaves like a brushed DC
motor: torque proportional to current, no commutator to wear out. That is
**Field-Oriented Control**, and it is why [Module 2](/sessions/02-motor.qmd)'s
$\tau = k_T I$ is usable at all.

The awkward part is that "90° ahead" is a statement about a *rotating* frame,
while the three phase currents live in a *stationary* one. FOC is mostly the
bookkeeping that moves between the two.

## Three objects, and what links them

The SimpleFOC architecture is built around three objects, each wrapping one piece of
hardware:

| Object | Wraps | Our hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `MagneticSensorSPI` | The angle sensor | AS5047P on SPI3 |
| `BLDCDriver6PWM` | The inverter | Six MOSFETs on the G431 |
| `BLDCMotor` | The control maths | --- |

`BLDCMotor` owns the algorithm and is told about the other two with
`linkSensor()` and `linkDriver()`. Nothing else connects them, which is why a
missing `link` call produces a motor that initialises cleanly and then does
nothing sensible.

## The two loops

Every iteration runs **two nested controllers**, and keeping them straight is
most of understanding the library:

- `motor.loopFOC()` --- the **inner** loop. Reads the angle, works out where
  the field should point, and sets the PWM duty cycles. It runs as fast as you
  can call it (above 10 kHz), and its rate is the loop frequency you read back with the
  commander's `F` command.
- `motor.move(target)` --- the **outer** loop. Turns your setpoint (a position,
  a speed, or a torque) into the q-axis demand the inner loop chases.

The inner loop is where speed matters; the outer loop is where tuning matters.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Both must be called every iteration

`loopFOC()` without `move()` holds whatever demand it last had. `move()`
without `loopFOC()` updates a number nothing acts on. Anything blocking in
`loop()` - a `delay()`, a slow `print` - drops the inner-loop rate and
shows up as a motor that runs rough at speed.
:::

## What the inner loop actually computes

Distilled from the library, with the bookkeeping removed:

```cpp
void loopFOC() {
  sensor.update();

  // 1. Mechanical angle -> electrical angle.
  //    A motor with p pole pairs turns through p electrical revolutions
  //    for every mechanical one. zero_electric_angle comes from initFOC().
  float angle_el = normalizeAngle(sensor.getAngle() * pole_pairs
                                  - zero_electric_angle);

  switch (torque_controller) {

    case TorqueControlType::voltage:
      // No current measurement. Ask for a voltage and hope; cheap and
      // adequate at low speed. This is where you start.
      Uq = target_voltage_q;
      Ud = 0;
      break;

    case TorqueControlType::foc_current:
      // 2. Measure two phase currents; the third follows from ia+ib+ic = 0.
      PhaseCurrent_s c = current_sense.getPhaseCurrents();

      // 3. Clarke (abc -> alpha/beta) then Park (alpha/beta -> d/q),
      //    using angle_el. The output is two DC values, not sinusoids.
      DQCurrent_s i = current_sense.getFOCCurrents(angle_el);

      // 4. Two independent PI controllers on those DC values.
      //    q is torque-producing; d is pure flux and is driven to zero
      //    because it costs current and produces nothing.
      Uq = PID_current_q(target_current_q - i.q);
      Ud = PID_current_d(0.0f - i.d);
      break;
  }

  setPhaseVoltage(Uq, Ud, angle_el);
}
```

The Park transform is the trick worth internalising. In the stationary frame
the phase currents are three sinusoids and there is nothing steady to control.
Rotating the frame with the rotor turns them into **two constants**, $i_d$ and
$i_q$, and a constant is something an ordinary PI controller can hold. Then you
rotate back:

```cpp
void setPhaseVoltage(float Uq, float Ud, float angle_el) {
  // Inverse Park: back to the stationary frame
  float Ualpha = Ud * cos(angle_el) - Uq * sin(angle_el);
  float Ubeta  = Ud * sin(angle_el) + Uq * cos(angle_el);

  // Inverse Clarke: two axes back to three phases
  float Ua = Ualpha;
  float Ub = -0.5f * Ualpha + _SQRT3_2 * Ubeta;
  float Uc = -0.5f * Ualpha - _SQRT3_2 * Ubeta;

  // Shift to sit around mid-rail, since the inverter cannot output
  // a negative voltage, then hand duty cycles to the hardware.
  driver.setPwm(Ua + Udc/2, Ub + Udc/2, Uc + Udc/2);
}
```

Setting $U_d = 0$ and driving only $U_q$ is exactly "put the field 90° ahead",
expressed in coordinates. Everything above is the machinery for saying it in
terms the three phases understand.

## What the outer loop computes

`move()` is a cascade, and which stages run depends on `motor.controller`:

```cpp
void move(float target) {
  switch (controller) {
    case MotionControlType::angle:
      // position -> velocity -> current, all three stages
      shaft_velocity_sp = P_angle(target - shaft_angle);
      target_current_q  = PID_velocity(shaft_velocity_sp - shaft_velocity);
      break;

    case MotionControlType::velocity:
      target_current_q  = PID_velocity(target - shaft_velocity);
      break;

    case MotionControlType::torque:
      target_current_q  = target;   // straight through
      break;
  }
}
```

This is why the commander's `T` means something different in each mode --- it
is the input to whichever stage is outermost. It is also why tuning proceeds
inside-out in [Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd): the velocity PI has to be
right before the position P above it can be.

## Alignment, and why the motor twitches at power-on

`motor.initFOC()` performs the one calibration FOC cannot do without. The
sensor reports *some* absolute angle, but nothing tells it how that number
relates to the motor's magnetic poles - that depends on how the magnet was
glued on and how the phase wires happened to be soldered. So `initFOC()` drives
a known field, watches which way the rotor moves and where it settles, and
stores two things:

- **`zero_electric_angle`** - the offset between sensor zero and electrical
  zero
- **sensor direction** - whether the sensor counts up or down relative to the
  motor's positive rotation

That is the twitch you see at every power-on. If it is skipped or wrong, the
field is placed at the wrong angle and the motor draws current while producing
little torque, or runs away.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why the UVW order does not matter

[Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd) says you can solder the phase wires in any
order. Swapping two phases reverses the motor's direction, and `initFOC()`
measures direction rather than assuming it - so the calibration simply comes
out with the other sign. The cost of getting it "wrong" is a stored constant,
not a rework.
:::

## The main ESC code

Setup is configuration; the loop is two calls. Trimmed to the parts that
matter:

```cpp
#include <SimpleFOC.h>

BLDCMotor motor = BLDCMotor(7);                 // pole pairs
BLDCDriver6PWM driver = BLDCDriver6PWM(A_PHASE_UH, A_PHASE_UL,
                                       A_PHASE_VH, A_PHASE_VL,
                                       A_PHASE_WH, A_PHASE_WL);
MagneticSensorSPI sensor = MagneticSensorSPI(AS5047_SPI, PA15);

float target = 0;

void setup() {
  sensor.init();
  motor.linkSensor(&sensor);

  driver.voltage_power_supply = 14.8;
  driver.init();
  motor.linkDriver(&driver);

  motor.foc_modulation = FOCModulationType::SpaceVectorPWM;
  motor.controller     = MotionControlType::velocity;

  motor.PID_velocity.P = 0.2;
  motor.PID_velocity.I = 20;
  motor.LPF_velocity.Tf = 0.01;   // velocity is differentiated, so filtered
  motor.voltage_limit   = 6;      // the safety net -- set it low first

  motor.init();
  motor.initFOC();                // alignment happens here
}

void loop() {
  motor.loopFOC();
  motor.move(target);
}
```

The pole-pair count must match the motor or every angle in the chain is wrong
by a fixed ratio, and the symptom is a motor that vibrates instead of turning.
`voltage_limit` is the one setting to get right before the first spin-up: it
caps what the inner loop can ask for regardless of what the outer loop demands.
